257.title: Workflow Automation
257.heading: Workflow Automation
257.content:
Workflow automation uses software and services to carry out repeatable process steps, transfer information, trigger later work, and check conditions with less manual coordination. A workflow can still contain human decisions where judgment or approval is required.

Automation improves consistency and scalability when the process and interfaces are well defined. Automating a redundant or poorly designed step can instead make the same waste occur faster, which is why process analysis should precede implementation.

260.title: Work
260.heading: Work
260.content: Work is energy transferred when a force acts through a displacement. For a constant force, $W=Fs\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between force and displacement. More generally, work is the integral of force along the path. The net work on a body equals its change in kinetic energy.

263.content:
Work in progress is all work that has begun but has not reached the workflow's completion state. High WIP creates queues, increases context switching, delays feedback, and hides the location of constraints.

Finishing a smaller number of items before starting others usually shortens [[Cycle Time]] and produces usable value sooner, even if fewer individuals appear continuously busy.

266.title: Work in Progress Limit
266.heading: Work in Progress Limit
266.content:
A work-in-progress limit caps how many items may occupy a workflow state or the system as a whole. When the limit is reached, the team helps finish or unblock existing work instead of introducing more.

The limit exposes a [[Bottleneck]] and changes behavior from individual busyness toward collective flow. It should be adjusted from measured results rather than used as an arbitrary quota.

Across software teams, excess work in progress often appears when one change requires coordination among several specialized groups. Items wait for prerequisites, are abandoned temporarily, and impose context-switching costs when resumed. Clear [[Bounded Context Ownership]] reduces those dependencies, while the limit makes remaining queues visible and encourages teams to finish work before starting more.

269.title: Word Embedding
269.heading: Word Embedding
269.content:
A word embedding represents a word as a dense numerical vector learned from patterns of use. Words that occur in similar contexts tend to receive nearby representations, providing a graded notion of semantic similarity.

Unlike one-hot identifiers, embeddings share statistical information among related words. They give language models and classifiers features that can generalize beyond phrases seen verbatim in a [[Training Dataset]].

Kelleher describes word2vec as learning vectors from neighboring-word co-occurrence: words used in similar textual contexts tend to acquire similar vectors. Those vectors can become numerical inputs to a [[Recurrent Neural Network]] for language processing. Proximity reflects patterns in a training corpus; it should not be mistaken for a complete account of a word's meaning in every context.

Deep feature engineering uses these learned vectors as distributed representations rather than sparse word identities. Recurrent, gated, and other sequence models can then operate on dense inputs whose geometry reflects corpus context.

271.heading: Document

272.sourceSearchName: word sequence representation word sequence representation
272.title: Word Sequence Representation
272.heading: Word Sequence Representation
272.content:
A word sequence representation tokenizes text into an ordered list of word occurrences. It moves beyond raw characters while preserving the order needed by language models, parsers, and other methods that infer relationships between neighboring or hierarchically combined words.

Tokenization and vocabulary decisions affect the result. Normalization and stop-word handling may reduce variation, but deleting or merging tokens can also remove grammatical or domain-specific information needed by a downstream task.

275.title: Wolfe Method
275.heading: Wolfe Method
275.content:
Wolfe's method solves a quadratic program by expressing its optimality and complementary-slackness conditions as a modified linear-programming tableau.

Artificial variables establish an initial basis, while restricted pivot choices preserve the paired slackness relationships. Under the method's convexity or concavity assumptions, the final feasible stationary point is optimal.

281.heading: Wireshark
281.content:
Wireshark is a packet capture and protocol analysis tool that displays network frames and decodes their layered fields. Filters can isolate a host, address, port, or protocol so an engineer can inspect one exchange among larger volumes of traffic.

The tool makes packet structure and timing visible, helping distinguish application errors from connection, routing, or protocol behavior. A capture should be collected only where authorized and stored as potentially sensitive data.

284.title: Windows Service
284.heading: Windows Service
284.content:
A Windows Service is a background application managed by the operating system and intended to run without an interactive user interface. The photo-storage project uses one to monitor a directory and upload files while the user is not actively running a desktop program.

A continuously running service consumes machine resources and is harder to inspect than an interactive application, so performance, logging, startup configuration, and clean shutdown matter. The .NET Core 3 example reaches the required Windows APIs through the [[Windows Compatibility Pack]].

The host's child-changed event gives the application access to the created UWP child so its data source and template can be configured. This separates the inter-framework bridge from the [[UWP TreeView Control]] that supplies the actual interface behavior.

290.content:
.NET Core 3.0 supported Windows Presentation Foundation as a Windows-only desktop framework. WPF combines XAML-defined interfaces with .NET code, data binding, styles, templates, and a vector-based rendering system.

Moving a WPF application to the newer runtime can modernize deployment and dependencies while preserving its desktop presentation model. Platform-specific integrations and third-party controls still require compatibility verification.

The .NET Core 3 migration discussion treats WPF alongside Windows Forms as an established Windows-only desktop model that can move to the newer runtime. It also presents XAML Islands as a way for WPF or Windows Forms hosts to incorporate selected UWP controls without replacing the whole application.

293.heading: Windows Forms on .NET Core
293.content:
.NET Core 3.0 brought Windows Forms support to the newer .NET runtime for Windows applications. Existing event-driven forms and controls could use modern project tooling while remaining tied to the Windows desktop environment.

Porting is not guaranteed to be a simple runtime switch because applications may depend on libraries or APIs absent from .NET Core. Compatibility analysis and targeted testing identify which pieces can move and which require replacement.

The Azure projects book demonstrates a 2019-era migration by changing a legacy Windows Forms project to the Windows Desktop SDK, targeting `netcoreapp3.0`, enabling Windows Forms, and then resolving package, reference, and resource differences. 296.content:
.NET supports several Windows desktop application models with different histories and capabilities. Windows Forms uses an event-driven control model, Windows Presentation Foundation uses XAML and a retained presentation system, and the Universal Windows Platform targets the modern Windows application platform.

Choosing among them depends on operating-system reach, existing code, UI requirements, deployment constraints, and access to platform APIs. Shared .NET libraries can preserve domain logic even when the presentation model is Windows-specific.

299.content:
The Windows Compatibility Pack provides additional APIs for .NET Core applications that run on Windows and need functionality familiar from the .NET Framework. It helps port code whose required operations are inherently tied to the Windows platform.

Adding the pack can reduce migration effort, but it does not make those APIs cross-platform. The dependency should be isolated and documented so portable application code is not accidentally coupled to Windows-specific behavior.

The photo-storage project uses the pack to recover Windows-specific APIs that were not part of the cross-platform .NET Core surface, including the APIs needed to implement a Windows Service. 305.content:
The Wilcoxon rank sum test compares two independent groups after replacing their combined measurements with ranks. It is equivalent to the Mann-Whitney test and avoids basing the comparison directly on sample means and standard deviations.

This rank-based construction can be less sensitive to extreme observations than a [[Student t-Test]]. It evaluates a distributional ordering rather than automatically testing equality of means, so interpretation depends on the shapes of the two group distributions.

Wicked problems persist because stakeholders have conflicting values and enough power to block unwanted proposals without enough agreement to establish a shared solution. More data or computing power cannot create the missing social consensus.

Computation can visualize consequences, compare scenarios, and support deliberation, but resolution requires cooperation and collective action. Recognizing this boundary prevents technical models from being mistaken for political decisions.

314.title: Wi-Fi
314.heading: Wi-Fi
314.content:
Wi-Fi provides wireless local-area networking over unlicensed radio spectrum. Access points connect nearby laptops and mobile devices to local networks and through them to the Internet.

Its limited range supports frequency reuse in homes, offices, and public spaces. Built-in laptop and smartphone support turned network access into an expected ambient service.

Whole game focus keeps every team oriented toward one integrated, playable build rather than a collection of locally optimized components. Each Sprint should demonstrate progress in that shared game.

A weighted residual finite element formulation substitutes an approximate field into a differential equation and forces the remaining residual to be orthogonal to selected weighting functions. It applies even when a convenient physical energy functional is unavailable.

Choosing the element shape functions as weights gives the Galerkin form. Integration can lower derivative requirements and introduces natural boundary terms before local equations are assembled.

323.title: Welch t-Test
323.heading: Welch t-Test
323.content:
The Welch t-test compares two independent means without assuming equal population variances. It adjusts the standard error and uses Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, which may be non-integer.

Many statistical systems use this test as the default two-sample t-test. When the equal- and unequal-variance analyses lead to the same substantive conclusion, the choice may not change the inference, but the reported method should remain explicit.

326.title: Whimsical Play
326.heading: Whimsical Play
326.content:
Whimsical play creates pleasure through silly actions, surprising consequences, bodily exuberance, or conceptual absurdity. Its rules often make an ordinary behavior strange enough that the sensation of performing it becomes the main event.

Whimsy can arise from constraint as readily as freedom. An awkward controller, deliberately unstable movement, or an implausible rule can produce a coherent experience when the resulting unpredictability supports the game's comic or euphoric character.

329.title: Weighted Input
329.heading: Weighted Input
329.content:
Weighted input is the sum obtained by multiplying each artificial-neuron input by its corresponding [[Neural Network Weight]] and adding the products. A [[Neural Network Bias]] is then added before the value enters the [[Activation Function]].

This calculation lets different connections influence the neuron by different amounts. Training changes the weights and bias, thereby changing how the same external input propagates through the network.

332.title: Weighted Graph
332.heading: Weighted Graph
332.content:
A weighted graph attaches a numerical value to each [[Edge]]. The value expresses a property of the represented relationship, such as distance, duration, cost, reward, or penalty.

Weights change how a route is evaluated: the [[Graph Path Length]] becomes the sum of edge weights rather than simply the number of edges. [[Dijkstra's Algorithm]] finds shortest paths when the relevant weights are nonnegative.

334.sourceSearchName: weighted decision matrix weighted decision matrix
334.title: Weighted Decision Matrix
334.heading: Document

335.sourceSearchName: weighted decision matrix weighted decision matrix
335.title: Weighted Decision Matrix
335.heading: Weighted Decision Matrix
335.content:
A weighted decision matrix compares alternatives by scoring each requirement and multiplying that score by the requirement's relative importance. The weighted results make explicit why one cloud service or vendor is preferred over another.

Weights distinguish critical factors from desirable ones, while scores record how fully each alternative satisfies them. The matrix supports judgment rather than replacing it, because poor criteria or unsupported scores merely give false precision to the decision.

336.title: Weighted Decision Matrix
336.heading: References

338.title: WebSurge
338.heading: WebSurge
338.content:
WebSurge is the load-testing tool used in the book to send a controlled volume of requests to an ASP.NET Core endpoint. Its measurements make changes in request throughput and response time visible during performance work.

The tool supplies evidence, not an explanation. Query count, server traces, and implementation details are still needed to identify why one version behaves differently from another.

A website entry page is the first page recorded for a visit or session. Entry-page analysis shows where users begin navigating and can identify prominent landing content.

It differs from total page views because a frequently viewed page may appear later in many sessions rather than initiating them.

344.title: WebRequest
344.heading: WebRequest
344.content:
`WebRequest` is a .NET request abstraction whose concrete implementation is selected from the URI scheme. It exposes common request configuration and execution behavior while subclasses handle protocol-specific details such as HTTP, FTP, or local files.

The abstraction illustrates a pluggable request model, although the book notes that some concrete request classes were already becoming obsolete in favor of newer clients. Code should not confuse a shared interface with identical protocol semantics.

346.heading: Document
346.content:

347.title: Weblog
347.heading: Weblog
347.content:
A weblog is a Web publication arranged as dated entries, typically with the newest material first and links to related sites. Publishing tools let writers post regularly without editing raw HTML.

Blogs lowered the technical barrier to writing on the Web and developed audiences around frequent personal commentary. Social platforms later absorbed some of their conversational role.

350.title: WebAssembly
350.heading: WebAssembly
350.content:
WebAssembly is a browser execution format for compiled code produced from languages other than JavaScript. The 2019 appendix presents it as a way for supported browsers to run portable, processor-oriented code while retaining the browser as the deployment environment.

WebAssembly expands the implementation choices available to a web application but does not replace every JavaScript or browser API interaction. The source emphasizes tradeoffs involving downloads, browser support, tooling, performance, and the amount of existing code that can be reused.

352.sourceSearchName: web assembly security sandbox web assembly security sandbox
352.title: WebAssembly Security Sandbox
352.heading: Document

353.sourceSearchName: web assembly security sandbox web assembly security sandbox
353.title: WebAssembly Security Sandbox
353.heading: WebAssembly Security Sandbox
353.content:
WebAssembly runs under the browser's security context rather than as an unrestricted executable installed directly on the user's computer. The source describes its security boundary as comparable to JavaScript because both rely on the browser sandbox.

The sandbox reduces direct machine access but does not make application logic or data automatically safe. Network requests, exposed secrets, untrusted inputs, and browser vulnerabilities still belong to the web application's security model.

354.sourceSearchName: web assembly security sandbox web assembly security sandbox
354.title: WebAssembly Security Sandbox
354.heading: References

355.sourceSearchName: web assembly performance web assembly performance
355.title: WebAssembly Performance
355.heading: Document

356.sourceSearchName: web assembly performance web assembly performance
356.title: WebAssembly Performance
356.heading: WebAssembly Performance
356.content:
WebAssembly performance is strongest for computation that benefits from compiled execution in the browser. The source cautions against a blanket claim that every WebAssembly application is faster than JavaScript because real performance includes startup and dependency costs.

A Blazor client, for example, must download the runtime and application assemblies before its C# code can execute locally. The workload and transfer profile therefore determine whether execution gains outweigh initialization cost.

357.title: WebAssembly Performance
357.heading: References

358.sourceSearchName: web assembly language portability web assembly language portability
358.title: WebAssembly Language Portability
358.heading: Document

359.sourceSearchName: web assembly language portability web assembly language portability
359.title: WebAssembly Language Portability
359.heading: WebAssembly Language Portability
359.content:
WebAssembly language portability allows code from supported compiled languages to target a common browser runtime format. A developer can use existing C or, through Blazor, C# knowledge for browser-side work instead of expressing all computation directly in JavaScript.

Portability depends on an appropriate compiler and the APIs available in the host. The benefit is greatest when a team can share language skills or application logic across server, client, mobile, and browser targets.

360.title: WebAssembly Language Portability
360.heading: References

361.sourceSearchName: web assembly deployment web assembly deployment
361.title: WebAssembly Deployment
361.heading: Document

362.sourceSearchName: web assembly deployment web assembly deployment
362.title: WebAssembly Deployment
362.heading: WebAssembly Deployment
362.content:
WebAssembly deployment delivers compiled application code through the web so the browser obtains the current version when it loads the site. This avoids many target-machine installation and update problems associated with conventional desktop software.

The model combines local browser execution with centralized web distribution. Download size remains a deployment concern, particularly when a client framework also ships a runtime and several assemblies.

363.sourceSearchName: web assembly deployment web assembly deployment
363.title: WebAssembly Deployment
363.heading: References

364.sourceSearchName: web assembly compilation web assembly compilation
364.title: WebAssembly Compilation
364.heading: Document

365.sourceSearchName: web assembly compilation web assembly compilation
365.title: WebAssembly Compilation
365.heading: WebAssembly Compilation
365.content:
WebAssembly compilation converts source written in a supported language into WASM that the browser can load and execute. The book uses WebAssembly Studio to build a small C example and inspect the generated output.

Compilation can catch source-language errors before deployment and provides an efficient browser execution target. It does not guarantee that the total application is faster because startup downloads and interactions with other libraries remain part of performance.

366.title: WebAssembly Compilation

367.sourceSearchName: web assembly code reuse web assembly code reuse
367.title: WebAssembly Code Reuse
367.heading: Document

368.sourceSearchName: web assembly code reuse web assembly code reuse
368.title: WebAssembly Code Reuse
368.heading: WebAssembly Code Reuse
368.content:
WebAssembly code reuse means an existing library or application written in a compilable language may be adapted to run in the browser rather than rewritten from the beginning in JavaScript. The appendix uses a C game as an example of a potentially portable existing codebase.

Reuse is not automatic because user interface, host integration, and unsupported dependencies may still need new adapters. The compiled core is most reusable when it is already separated from operating-system-specific behavior.

369.sourceSearchName: web assembly code reuse web assembly code reuse

374.content:
Web-based AR authoring applies web content and linking ideas to registered spatial information. A physical artifact can be associated with virtual content, while markup, style, and localization attributes describe what appears and how it is arranged.

An AR browser can combine several content channels rather than allowing one application to monopolize the display. Composition and view management must resolve competition for limited visual space and preserve the source and meaning of each channel.

377.heading: Web Views and Visits
377.content:
Web views count page-level display events, whereas visits group related activity into sessions. One visit can produce many views, so the two measures answer different questions about reach and engagement.

Sessionization rules and bot filtering must be stated before comparing visit counts over time.

380.heading: Web Snippet Clustering
380.content:
Web snippet clustering organizes short search-result descriptions into coherent topical groups. The method must work with sparse text, duplicated language, noisy markup, and ambiguous queries while producing labels quickly enough for interactive use.

Phrase extraction, background knowledge, and overlap-tolerant clustering help distinguish different senses of a query. Good labels are part of the result because users need to understand each cluster before choosing which results to inspect.

383.title: Web Server
383.heading: Web Server
383.content:
A web server listens for network requests and passes them into a web application. It is distinct from the [[Web Host]], which provides the broader execution context and application services.

ASP.NET Core can use servers such as [[Kestrel]] and can also integrate with an external server such as [[Internet Information Services]] or operate behind an [[Nginx]] [[Reverse Proxy]].

386.heading: Web Portal
386.content:
A Web portal collects search, news, mail, discussion, entertainment, and other services on one page. It aims to become a user’s starting point and retain attention within a curated environment.

Advertising supported many portals during the dot-com boom. Their incentive to keep visitors could conflict with the search function that sent users elsewhere.

389.content:
A web of trust derives confidence through a network of participants who vouch for one another. Direct trust can be extended along paths to estimate whether an unknown contributor or item should be believed.

Trust propagation must limit path length, cycles, collusion, and the influence of uncertain intermediaries. A dense connection graph is not automatically evidence of honest behavior.

392.title: Web Mercator Projection
392.heading: Web Mercator Projection
392.content: Web Mercator is the projected coordinate system widely used by tiled online maps. It supports a consistent square tile pyramid and familiar pan-and-zoom behavior, but it increasingly enlarges area toward the poles and is not suitable for accurate global area comparison. Thematic layers commonly require [[Spatial Data Reprojection]] before being placed over Web Mercator tiles. That alignment does not remove the projection's distortions.

393.title: Web Mercator Projection

395.title: Web Host
395.heading: Web Host
395.content:
A web host is the execution context of an ASP.NET Core web application. It coordinates application startup and supplies web-related hosting services rather than directly representing the network listener.

Host construction can select the [[Kestrel]] [[Web Server]], set the content root used to find configuration, enable IIS integration, identify the startup class, and then build and run the configured application.

398.title: Web Graph
398.heading: Web Graph
398.content:
The web graph represents each web page as a [[Vertex]] and each [[Hyperlink]] as a directed [[Edge]]. A page can link to another without receiving a link back, so the structure is a [[Directed Graph]].

This model turns the enormous scale of the web into usable information. [[PageRank]] derives relative page importance from patterns of outgoing links, backlinks, dangling nodes, and connected groups within the graph.

401.title: Web Form
401.heading: Web Form
401.content:
A web form collects user values and submits them for an application operation. A useful form must provide understandable controls and feedback while also producing data the application can validate and process.

Angular can represent a form through a template-driven or reactive model. Regardless of the client approach, the server must repeat essential validation because the browser-side form can be bypassed or altered.

404.title: Web Deploy
404.heading: Web Deploy
404.content:
Web Deploy is a publishing target for transferring and synchronizing a web application's deployment content with a compatible server. Visual Studio can store the destination and build choices in a publish profile for repeatable releases.

The target automates movement of application artifacts, not the correctness of the destination environment. Server configuration, database access, application settings, and credentials still have to match the published build.

406.sourceSearchName: web deploy package web deploy package
406.title: Web Deploy Package
406.heading: Document

407.sourceSearchName: web deploy package web deploy package
407.title: Web Deploy Package
407.heading: Web Deploy Package
407.content:
A Web Deploy package is a portable deployment artifact produced for later installation through Web Deploy rather than sent immediately to a live destination. It separates package creation from the moment and credentials of deployment.

This is useful when another operator or environment owns the release step. The package must still correspond to the target's runtime and configuration expectations.

408.sourceSearchName: web deploy package web deploy package
408.title: Web Deploy Package
408.heading: References

410.title: Web Crawler
410.heading: Web Crawler
410.content:
A web crawler systematically follows [[Hyperlink|hyperlinks]] to discover and read web pages. Search engines use crawling to collect the documents and connections that can later be indexed and searched.

Crawling and ranking are separate tasks. The crawler supplies page content and link structure, a [[Search Engine Index]] supports matching a query, and [[PageRank]] can help order the matched pages by relative importance.

413.heading: Web Content Management System
413.content:
A web content management system lets editors create, organize, revise, and publish site content through an application rather than by changing source code. It typically separates structured content from templates that determine how that content is rendered.

CMS design balances editorial flexibility with a controlled information model. Content types, fields, media, permissions, routes, and presentation templates establish what editors can express and how reliably the site can deliver it.

416.title: Web Commercialization
416.heading: Web Commercialization
416.content:
Web commercialization transformed an open research information system into a platform for retail, advertising, finance, and subscription services. Secure browsers, user sessions, household access, and relaxed network policies made transactions practical.

Companies such as Amazon and eBay demonstrated new business models while speculative investment produced the dot-com bubble. The market crash removed many firms without reversing commercial use of the Web.

The Web Chat channel provides a browser-based interface for interacting with a registered bot. It is available as a convenient way to verify the deployed bot without first building a custom client.

Web Chat and Direct Line are two interfaces to the same bot service. The channel changes how users connect, not the intent recognition and response logic running behind the messaging endpoint.

422.content:
A Web browser requests resources identified by URLs, interprets HTML and related formats, and presents linked information for navigation. Berners-Lee created an early browser along with the Web’s protocols.

Graphical browsers integrated images, typography, icons, and mouse input. They turned Internet access from a specialist activity into a widely usable information environment.

428.content:
A Web App Manifest is a JSON file describing install-related metadata for a web application. It identifies values such as the application name, short name, start URL, display behavior, and icon set.

A page links to the manifest so the browser can recognize the site as an application and create an installed entry or home-screen icon. The manifest complements rather than replaces the [[Service Worker]].

431.title: Web API
431.heading: Web API
431.content:
A Web API is a programmatic set of server-side endpoints exposed through HTTP or HTTPS. Each endpoint accepts a defined request and returns a response represented in a format such as JSON.

In ASP.NET Core, [[MVC Controller|controller]] actions commonly implement these endpoints. An Angular [[Single-Page Application]] calls them to obtain or modify data without requiring the server to render the client interface.

433.heading: Document

434.sourceSearchName: web analytics data quality web analytics data quality
434.title: Web Analytics Data Quality
434.heading: Web Analytics Data Quality
434.content:
Web analytics data quality concerns whether logs and derived fields consistently represent real user activity. Missing identifiers, duplicate events, bot traffic, internal requests, malformed timestamps, and changing instrumentation can distort conclusions.

Quality review should precede aggregation so apparently precise charts do not merely summarize collection artifacts.

435.sourceSearchName: web analytics data quality web analytics data quality

437.title: Web 4.0
437.heading: Web 4.0
437.content:
Web 4.0 is presented as an evolution toward a more intelligent, connected, and interactive web in which systems and people exchange information continuously. It provides a network environment for data-rich services and automated responses.

The label is a stage model used by the source, not a single technical standard. Its importance lies in the convergence of artificial intelligence, mobile access, connected devices, and business analytics.

440.sourceSearchName: weak regular sequence weak regular sequence
440.title: Weak Regular Sequence
440.heading: Weak Regular Sequence
440.content:
A weak regular sequence satisfies the successive non-zero-divisor conditions of a [[Regular Sequence]] but does not require the final quotient M/(r₁,…,rₙ)M to be nonzero.

The distinction matters under scalar extension: flatness preserves weak regularity, while an additional nontriviality condition is needed to obtain a regular sequence. Faithful flatness reflects both properties.

443.heading: Weak Computational View of Nature
443.content:
The weak computational view holds that computational models are useful tools for studying the world without claiming that the world itself is a computer. A phenomenon may behave as if it were an information process for the purposes of explanation and prediction.

This position evaluates computational interpretations by their evidence and usefulness. It preserves a distinction between a model and the reality the model represents.

446.title: Waypoint Indicator
446.heading: Waypoint Indicator
446.content:
A waypoint indicator converts the world position of a destination into a visual cue that helps the player locate it. A visible waypoint can be projected directly onto the screen, while an off-screen target requires an edge marker or directional arrow.

The implementation must account for targets behind the camera and clamp cues to a useful screen region. Distance or contextual labels can supplement direction without overwhelming the view.

448.title: Wayfinding
448.heading: Document
448.content:
2026-09-05 13:11

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Spatial Perception and Navigation]] [[Augmented Reality Navigation]]

449.title: Wayfinding
449.heading: Wayfinding
449.content:
Wayfinding is the cognitive process of determining and following a route between an origin and a destination. It is the planning and decision-making component of [[Navigation]].

The user determines the current location, selects a path, maintains orientation, and builds or consults a [[Cognitive Map]]. Wayfinding aids support this mental work rather than moving the user directly. Examples include maps, signs, trails, compasses, reference objects, and [[Landmark]]s.

In a large or unfamiliar [[Virtual Environment]], wayfinding aids can be essential even when the [[3D Travel]] technique is efficient. Integrated aids can reduce [[Cognitive Load]] and strengthen [[Spatial Knowledge]].

An [[AR Route Visualization]] can place a path or decision cue directly onto the traveler's view of the physical environment. This reduces the transformation required from a separate map, but the route should still expose useful landmarks and orientation so the user does not become dependent on following an isolated arrow.

452.title: Wavelet Transform
452.heading: Wavelet Transform
452.content:
A wavelet transform decomposes a signal into components associated with different scales or frequency ranges while retaining localized information. Approximation components capture broader movement and detail components capture finer variation.

This multiscale representation can separate structure from noise before forecasting. The choice of wavelet and decomposition depth determines which patterns are exposed to later learning.

455.title: Wavefront OBJ and MTL Format
455.heading: Wavefront OBJ and MTL Format
455.content:
Wavefront OBJ is a human-readable interchange format for mesh geometry. It can declare vertices, texture coordinates, normals, and faces that index those collections. Its companion MTL file describes material-related information referenced by the model.

OBJ's indexed faces can reuse a vertex across several polygons and can represent faces with more than three coplanar points. This makes the format relatively compact and understandable, while its deliberately limited scope also makes it more portable than an application-native project file.

458.title: Wavelet Thresholding
458.heading: Wavelet Thresholding
458.content:
Wavelet thresholding modifies or removes small wavelet coefficients after a [[Wavelet Transform]] to reduce noise. Coefficients below a selected threshold are treated as less informative than the larger components that represent stronger signal structure.

The threshold controls a tradeoff: aggressive removal simplifies the signal but may discard useful detail, while a weak threshold leaves more noise for the forecasting model.

461.title: WaveCluster
461.heading: WaveCluster
461.content:
WaveCluster quantizes the feature space and applies a wavelet transform to the resulting grid. The transform suppresses small fluctuations and highlights connected high-density regions at selected scales.

Because wavelets separate signal by scale, the method can find irregular clusters and reduce sensitivity to point-level noise. Grid resolution and the chosen transform scale determine whether nearby regions remain distinct or merge.

463.sourceSearchName: wave particle duality wave particle duality
463.title: Wave-Particle Duality
463.heading: Document

464.sourceSearchName: wave particle duality wave particle duality
464.title: Wave-Particle Duality
464.heading: Wave-Particle Duality
464.content: Wave-particle duality describes quantum entities through both wave-like interference and particle-like localized detection. Which behavior becomes evident depends on the experimental arrangement. The two descriptions are not classical alternatives carried simultaneously in ordinary form; quantum theory uses a state amplitude to predict probabilities for discrete outcomes.

465.sourceSearchName: wave particle duality wave particle duality
465.title: Wave-Particle Duality
465.heading: References

467.title: Wave Superposition
467.heading: Wave Superposition
467.content: The principle of superposition states that when compatible waves overlap, the resultant disturbance is the vector sum of their individual disturbances. In-phase contributions reinforce through constructive interference, while opposite-phase contributions cancel through destructive interference. After overlapping in a linear medium, the component waves continue with their original forms.

469.title: Wave Intensity
469.heading: Document

2026-09-17 00:04

470.title: Wave Intensity
470.heading: Wave Intensity
470.content: Wave intensity is power transferred per unit area. For a harmonic wave in a fixed medium, intensity is proportional to the square of amplitude, so doubling amplitude multiplies intensity by four. For energy spreading uniformly from a point source, the growing spherical area produces an [[Inverse-Square Law]] with distance.

472.sourceSearchName: water gas shift reaction water gas shift reaction
472.title: Water-Gas Shift Reaction
472.heading: Document

473.sourceSearchName: water gas shift reaction water gas shift reaction
473.title: Water-Gas Shift Reaction
473.heading: Water-Gas Shift Reaction
473.content: The water-gas shift reaction converts carbon monoxide and steam into carbon dioxide and additional hydrogen: $CO+H_2O\rightarrow CO_2+H_2$. In the source's natural-gas hydrogen route, catalytic high- and lower-temperature stages reduce CO before CO2 scrubbing. This step increases recovered hydrogen and changes the gas composition; it does not create hydrogen without an upstream feedstock and heat supply.

474.sourceSearchName: water gas shift reaction water gas shift reaction
474.title: Water-Gas Shift Reaction
474.heading: References

476.title: Water Electrolysis
476.heading: Water Electrolysis
476.content: Water electrolysis uses electrical energy to separate water into hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode. The source describes alkaline, membrane, and high-temperature steam versions and gives the net reaction as $2H_2O+energy\rightarrow2H_2+O_2$. If electricity comes from intermittent solar or wind supply, produced hydrogen can shift some of that energy into a stored fuel for later use.

479.title: Watchdog Process
479.heading: Watchdog Process
479.content:
A watchdog process actively tests known failure points in another application or service. It can call a health endpoint on a schedule, compare the result with expected thresholds, and notify or initiate recovery when the service is unhealthy.

The watchdog should run outside the component it observes so that the same failure does not silence both. Its checks must represent meaningful dependencies rather than merely prove that one process can return a successful response.

482.title: Wartime Secrecy and Technology Transfer
482.heading: Wartime Secrecy and Technology Transfer
482.content:
Military secrecy shaped which computing innovations entered public knowledge and commercial production after World War II. British codebreaking machines remained hidden, while American projects more readily seeded companies, government laboratories, and university programs.

Secrecy protected continuing cryptographic capabilities but distorted historical credit and slowed reuse. Technology transfer depended as much on institutions and policy as on the technical quality of a machine.

484.title: Ward's Method

485.sourceSearchName: ward s method ward s method
485.title: Ward's Method
485.heading: Ward's Method
485.content:
Ward's method merges the two clusters that cause the smallest increase in within-cluster error sum of squares. It treats the loss of information from a merge as the objective to minimize.

The greedy rule often produces compact, roughly spherical clusters. Like other agglomerative methods, it cannot undo an earlier merge even if a later global comparison suggests a different structure.

486.title: Ward's Method
486.heading: References

488.title: Wald Test
488.heading: Wald Test
488.content:
A Wald test evaluates whether an estimated model coefficient differs from a hypothesized value, usually zero, by comparing the estimate with its standard error. Logistic regression output commonly reports a z or chi-squared form of this test.

The test supports variable-selection decisions but can behave poorly for unstable or extreme estimates. Confidence intervals and model comparisons provide additional context, especially near separation or with sparse categories.

491.title: Wake Word
491.heading: Wake Word
491.content:
A wake word is a short activation phrase that tells a listening device to begin processing a request. Detection can run locally so that continuous ambient audio does not need to be sent to a remote [[Speech-to-Text Service]].

A device can maintain only a short rolling audio buffer and transmit speech after a likely activation. This design reduces unnecessary network processing, although false activations and privacy expectations still require care.

493.sourceSearchName: von neumann architecture von neumann architecture
493.title: Von Neumann Architecture

493.content:
2026-09-13 20:16

Tags: [[Computing Machine Architecture]] · [[Stored-Program and Mainframe Computing]]

494.sourceSearchName: von neumann architecture von neumann architecture
494.title: Von Neumann Architecture
494.heading: Von Neumann Architecture
494.content:
The von Neumann architecture organizes a computer around a central processing unit, memory, and input-output subsystem. The CPU follows a sequence of instructions stored in memory and exchanges data with that memory as it works.

The architecture gives physical meaning to familiar programming ideas such as sequential steps, branches, and variables. Its separation of processing and memory also creates the [[Processor-Memory Bottleneck]].

495.title: Von Neumann Architecture
495.heading: References

496.title: Waiting Time Prediction
496.heading: Document

497.sourceSearchName: waiting time prediction waiting time prediction
497.title: Waiting Time Prediction
497.heading: Waiting Time Prediction
497.content:
Waiting time prediction estimates how long a person will remain in a queue before service begins. The hospital approach sums predicted treatment durations for patients ahead while accounting for the current task state.

Uncertainty grows with queue length because individual duration errors accumulate, arrivals and priorities change, and real operations do not follow a fixed schedule exactly.

498.sourceSearchName: waiting time prediction waiting time prediction
498.title: Waiting Time Prediction
498.heading: References

Tags: [[.NET Task Parallelism and Asynchrony]]

500.sourceSearchName: waiting for .net tasks waiting for .net tasks
500.title: Waiting for .NET Tasks
500.heading: Waiting for .NET Tasks
500.content:
.NET can wait for one task, any task in a set, or every task in a set. Synchronous APIs such as `Wait`, `WaitAny`, and `WaitAll` block the calling thread, whereas asynchronous waiting allows the caller to yield until completion.

The wait shape should match the dependency: continue after the first useful result, after all required results, or after one specific operation. Blocking is especially risky in responsive and server applications because it consumes a thread and may participate in a deadlock.

501.sourceSearchName: waiting for .net tasks waiting for .net tasks
501.title: Waiting for .NET Tasks
501.heading: References

503.title: VOR Navigation
503.heading: VOR Navigation
503.content: Very High Frequency Omnidirectional Range navigation lets an aircraft determine its bearing, or radial, relative to a ground station. The station transmits a reference signal and a direction-dependent rotating pattern; their phase relationship identifies direction from the facility. Networks of VOR stations became waypoints for established air routes, but their VHF signals remain limited largely to line of sight and therefore depend on ground infrastructure and terrain clearance.

505.sourceSearchName: volumetric flow rate conversion volumetric flow rate conversion
505.title: Volumetric Flow Rate Conversion

506.title: Volumetric Flow Rate Conversion
506.heading: Volumetric Flow Rate Conversion
506.content: Volumetric flow combines volume with inverse time, such as ft³/s or L/day. The book converts cubic feet per second to cubic meters per second with a volume ratio because the seconds already match. When the time unit differs, a second factor must be oriented to cancel the denominator as well. The app lists per-second, per-minute, and per-day choices, illustrating why a flow result cannot be obtained from a volume factor alone in every case. See [[Volume Unit Scaling]] and [[Compound Rate Unit Conversion]].

509.title: Von Mises Stress
509.heading: Von Mises Stress
509.content:
Von Mises stress combines components of a multiaxial stress state into one equivalent scalar. It is commonly plotted in finite element post-processing to compare spatial stress intensity and identify critical regions.

For a plate with a hole, the distribution highlights the concentration around the boundary. Numerical maxima should be checked against analytical stress-concentration estimates and equilibrium.

512.title: Volumetric Heat Capacity
512.heading: Volumetric Heat Capacity
512.content:
Specific heat capacity measures energy required to raise a unit mass by one degree, while density converts that mass-based quantity to energy storage per unit volume. Their product $\rho c_p$ is the volumetric heat capacity used in transient heat equations.

A high value lets a region absorb more energy for the same temperature rise. Together with conductivity it determines [[Thermal Diffusivity from Material Properties|thermal diffusivity]], separating a material's ability to store thermal energy from its ability to redistribute it.
